topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
summary: This topic examines foundational Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) models that govern software engineering from initial feasibility to final decommissioning. It details the classical linear Waterfall model and its rigid phase-gate milestones, the V-Model with its early verification/validation mapping between development and testing tiers, the Prototyping model (throwaway vs evolutionary) and its critical role in resolving requirements ambiguity, Iterative and Incremental delivery, Barry Boehm's risk-driven Spiral Model with its four cyclic quadrants, and the Rational Unified Process (RUP) with its four distinct phases (Inception, Elaboration, Construction, Transition). Formal criteria for selecting optimal process models based on requirements stability, project risk, and organizational constraints are emphasized.

key_terms.definition: A structured framework defining the distinct phases involved in planning, creating, testing, deploying, and maintaining a software system.
A linear-sequential process model where development proceeds sequentially through defined phases (requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance) with sign-off gates.
A development lifecycle model establishing direct 1-to-1 correspondence between each development phase on the downward arm and its corresponding testing phase on the upward arm.
A process model focused on building early mock-ups or working representations of a system to elicit, clarify, and validate user requirements.
A risk-driven iterative lifecycle model developed by Barry Boehm that couples iterative development with systematic risk analysis across four radial quadrants.
An architecture-centric, use-case driven iterative process framework structured into four sequential phases: Inception, Elaboration, Construction, and Transition.
A prototype developed rapidly to clarify requirements or explore design alternatives and then discarded rather than becoming the basis for production software.
An initial investigation assessing the technical, economic, operational, schedule, and legal viability of a proposed software project.

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 3: What is the key defining feature of the Spiral Model?
options: Risk assessment and management at every iteration
Elimination of all documentation
Strict sequential phase completion without review
Exclusively pair programming
questions.answer: Risk assessment and management at every iteration
questions.explanation: As tested in Nile Exam Question 3: Barry Boehm's Spiral Model is fundamentally a risk-driven process model. Unlike linear or purely agile models, every single 360-degree spiral loop explicitly begins with setting objectives and mandates an in-depth risk analysis step to identify and resolve technical, financial, or operational risks before engineering proceeds.

why_wrong.Elimination of all documentation: The Spiral Model produces formal documentation, milestone reviews, and management checkpoints at each loop.
This is the Waterfall model, whereas the Spiral model is inherently iterative and cyclic.
why_wrong.Exclusively pair programming: Pair programming is a practice of Extreme Programming (XP), not the Spiral Model.

marking_points: Identifies risk assessment/management as defining feature
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 3

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 4: Which phase of the Waterfall Model focuses on creating detailed requirements and system specifications?
options: Requirements analysis and specification
System design
Implementation
Maintenance
questions.explanation: In the classical Waterfall Model, detailed functional and non-functional requirements are gathered, analyzed, and documented in a formal Software Requirements Specification (SRS) during the Requirements Analysis phase before any design or coding begins.

why_wrong.System design: Design focuses on creating the architectural blueprint, data structures, and algorithms to satisfy already-defined requirements.
why_wrong.Implementation: Implementation translates detailed design into executable source code.
why_wrong.Maintenance: Maintenance occurs post-deployment to patch defects and handle environmental changes.

questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 4

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 10: What is the main goal of prototyping in software development?
options: Validation and refinement of requirements with stakeholders
Rapid delivery of the final production system
Reducing the need for software testing
Simplifying the compiler optimization process
questions.answer: Validation and refinement of requirements with stakeholders
questions.explanation: The primary objective of building a prototype is to clarify ambiguous user requirements, validate user interface workflows, and resolve stakeholder misunderstandings early in the development lifecycle before committing major resources to production engineering.

why_wrong.Rapid delivery of the final production s: Prototypes are typically throwaway or preliminary models, not hardened production-ready systems.
why_wrong.Reducing the need for software testing: Testing remains mandatory; prototypes do not eliminate formal verification and validation.
why_wrong.Simplifying the compiler optimization pr: Compilers optimize binaries independently of development process models.

questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 10

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 15: What is the main focus of the Rational Unified Process (RUP)?
options: Iterative development and architecture-centric management of requirements
Strict adherence to a linear waterfall sequence
Writing code without any software architecture
Manual testing without automated tools
questions.answer: Iterative development and architecture-centric management of requirements
questions.explanation: RUP is an iterative and incremental process framework characterized as being: 1. Use-case driven; 2. Architecture-centric (establishing an executable architectural baseline in the Elaboration phase); and 3. Iterative and risk-focused.

why_wrong.Strict adherence to a linear waterfall s: RUP explicitly rejects single-pass waterfall development in favor of iterative cycles.
why_wrong.Writing code without any software archit: RUP is famously architecture-centric, emphasizing early architectural stabilization.
why_wrong.Manual testing without automated tools: RUP strongly emphasizes automated test suites.

questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 15

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 43: Prototyping is valuable during requirements elicitation primarily because it helps:
options: Reveal hidden assumptions and misunderstandings through tangible visual and interactive demonstration
Replace the need for any formal written requirements documentation
Force developers to begin writing production database queries early
Eliminate the need to involve real end-users
questions.answer: Reveal hidden assumptions and misunderstandings through tangible visual and interactive demonstration
questions.explanation: Users frequently struggle to articulate abstract needs from text documents. An interactive prototype allows stakeholders to test workflows directly, exposing unstated assumptions, missing validation rules, and conflicting expectations while changes are cheap to make.

why_wrong.Replace the need for any formal written: A prototype supplements, but does not entirely replace, formal contractual specifications.
why_wrong.Force developers to begin writing produc: Prototypes often use mock data; forcing early production DB design defeats the exploratory purpose.
why_wrong.Eliminate the need to involve real end-u: Prototypes are built specifically to engage real end-users.

marking_points: Reveals hidden assumptions through interactive visual demonstration
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 43

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: Match each testing level in the V-Model with the specific development phase it directly validates:
options: Acceptance Testing -> Requirements Analysis; System Testing -> System Architecture Design; Integration Testing -> Detailed Subsystem Design; Unit Testing -> Component Implementation
Acceptance Testing -> Implementation; Unit Testing -> Requirements Analysis
System Testing -> Feasibility Study; Unit Testing -> Maintenance
Integration Testing -> Deployment; Acceptance Testing -> Database Schema
questions.answer: Acceptance Testing -> Requirements Analysis; System Testing -> System Architecture Design; Integration Testing -> Detailed Subsystem Design; Unit Testing -> Component Implementation
questions.explanation: In the V-Model: 1. Unit Testing validates the low-level code and component logic; 2. Integration Testing validates detailed module interfaces; 3. System Testing validates high-level architectural integration; 4. Acceptance Testing validates user requirements against the original specification.

Feasibility is a planning activity, not a direct software verification artifact.
Integration occurs prior to system testing and deployment.

questions.source: Software Engineering Process Models Lecture Notes, Section 5

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: In the Rational Unified Process (RUP), during which of the four sequential phases is the baseline executable software architecture established and major risks mitigated?
options: Elaboration Phase
Inception Phase
Construction Phase
Transition Phase
questions.explanation: RUP defines four phases: 1. Inception (establish business case and scope); 2. Elaboration (analyze problem domain, establish architectural baseline, resolve highest risks); 3. Construction (bulk coding and component integration); 4. Transition (deploying to users).

why_wrong.Inception Phase: Inception defines project scope, business viability, and initial cost estimates, not the full architecture.
why_wrong.Construction Phase: Construction builds the remaining functionality upon the already-established architectural baseline.
why_wrong.Transition Phase: Transition handles beta testing, user training, and deployment.

marking_points: Identifies Elaboration phase as establishing architectural baseline
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 5 & RUP Standards

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: What is the primary risk of using a pure Waterfall Model for a software project where customer requirements are vague or likely to change?
options: Late changes are extremely costly and working software is not available until near the end of the project lifecycle, leading to catastrophic late-stage project failure.
Developers will write code too quickly without understanding requirements.
The Waterfall Model cannot be used with relational databases.
Waterfall requires zero documentation, leaving no audit trail.
questions.answer: Late changes are extremely costly and working software is not available until near the end of the project lifecycle, leading to catastrophic late-stage project failure.
questions.explanation: Because Waterfall requires freezing requirements before design and coding, changing requirements mid-way requires discarding completed work. Testing happens at the end ('big bang'), meaning major conceptual misunderstandings are discovered too late.

Waterfall delays coding until requirements and design are fully documented.
why_wrong.The Waterfall Model cannot be used with: Waterfall has been used with databases for decades.

marking_points: Working software only appears at the end
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 5.1

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: What is the Waterfall Model?

questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
questions.question: What is the difference between Throwaway and Evolutionary prototyping?
questions.answer:
- Throwaway: Built quickly to clarify requirements and then discarded.
- Evolutionary: Starts with core verified requirements and is progressively refined into the final production system.
questions.explanation: Distinguished by whether the prototype codebase survives into production.

questions.answer:
1. Determine objectives and constraints
2. Evaluate alternatives and assess/resolve risks

case_studies.scenario: A federal government ministry in Abuja contracts an IT consulting consortium to develop a nationwide e-Passport and border control management system. The project involves strict biometric encryption protocols, multi-agency legal clearances, integration with international police databases, and life-critical security compliance. The ministry's senior director demands using a pure 2-week Agile sprint model, while the systems architect argues for a risk-driven Spiral Model.

sub_questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
sub_questions.question: Why is the Spiral Model or a hybrid RUP approach technically superior to a pure rapid-fire Agile sprint model for this national security system?
options: Because the project carries severe technical, legal, and national security risks that require explicit risk assessment, formal architectural baselines, and verification gates before full-scale deployment.
Because the Spiral Model guarantees that software will be built with zero lines of code.
Because Agile methodologies are illegal under Nigerian copyright law.
Because the Waterfall model cannot run on Linux servers.
sub_questions.answer: Because the project carries severe technical, legal, and national security risks that require explicit risk assessment, formal architectural baselines, and verification gates before full-scale deployment.
sub_questions.explanation: Large-scale safety-critical systems with strict regulatory compliance, multi-agency dependencies, and catastrophic failure penalties require formal risk mitigation, comprehensive documentation, and architectural verification (strengths of the Spiral Model and RUP Elaboration), which purely informal Agile sprints can overlook.

why_wrong.Because the Spiral Model guarantees zero: Nonsensical assertion; software must be coded.
Agile is an engineering management philosophy, not a statutory offense.
why_wrong.Because the Waterfall model cannot run o: Process models are management frameworks, independent of the operating system.

marking_points: Emphasizes risk assessment and architectural baseline requirements

sub_questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
sub_questions.question: Outline how the consulting team would execute one complete 360-degree spiral loop for the 'Biometric Facial Recognition Subsystem' across the four quadrants of the Spiral Model.
sub_questions.answer:
1. Quadrant 1 (Objectives & Constraints): Define requirements for facial recognition accuracy (e.g. false match rate < 0.001%), target processing speed (< 1.5 seconds per passenger), and international ICAO standards.
2. Quadrant 2 (Risk Assessment & Mitigation): Identify major risks (e.g. poor airport lighting, sensor latency, demographic bias). Build an experimental prototype and run simulations with diverse image sets to assess and mitigate these risks.
3. Quadrant 3 (Development & Verification): Design the production algorithms, integrate camera drivers, write test harnesses, and execute formal verification against benchmark passport photos.
4. Quadrant 4 (Planning & Review): Review test outcomes with ministry security stakeholders, evaluate budget/schedule, and plan the next spiral cycle (e.g. integrating fingerprint sensors).
sub_questions.explanation: Demonstrates practical operationalization of Boehm's four quadrants on an authentic high-risk subsystem.
marking_points: Quadrant 1: Sets objectives, metrics, and constraints
Quadrant 2: Identifies risks (lighting, bias) and builds prototype to mitigate
Quadrant 3: Develops and verifies the subsystem
Quadrant 4: Reviews with stakeholders and plans next cycle

case_studies.scenario: A development team at Nile University Hospital builds an interactive web-based prototype in two weeks using a low-code UI builder to demonstrate how doctors will enter prescription orders. Hospital administrators are so impressed by the polished visual interface that they instruct the IT department to deploy the prototype immediately to live patient wards on Monday, canceling the planned 6-month backend engineering budget.

sub_questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
sub_questions.question: What classic software engineering hazard (the 'Prototyping Trap') does this scenario illustrate?
options: Management mistaking an unhardened, non-secure throwaway prototype with mock data for production-ready software.
The prototype running out of memory due to C language pointer errors.
The hospital violating open-source GPL licenses.
Developers spending too much time on automated unit tests.
sub_questions.answer: Management mistaking an unhardened, non-secure throwaway prototype with mock data for production-ready software.
sub_questions.explanation: As warned in Section 5.2 of the lecture notes: A primary risk of prototyping is that stakeholders see a functioning visual screen and assume the software is complete. In reality, the prototype lacks database ACID transactions, patient data encryption, audit logging, input sanitization, and concurrent error handling, creating grave patient safety hazards.

The issue is architectural and managerial, not low-level pointer management.
why_wrong.The hospital violating open-source GPL l: Licensing is irrelevant to the core hazard described.
The team built a quick UI mockup without backend tests.

marking_points: Identifies mistaking throwaway UI mockup for production-ready system
sub_questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 5.2

sub_questions.topic: Software Process Models: Prescriptive, Iterative & Risk-Driven
sub_questions.question: List four vital engineering qualities that are typically absent from a rapid throwaway UI prototype that must be built before live medical deployment.
sub_questions.answer:
1. Data Security & Privacy: Encryption of sensitive patient health records at rest and in transit, and role-based access control.
2. Concurrency & Transactional Integrity: ACID database transactions preventing duplicate prescriptions if two nurses click simultaneously.
3. Fault Tolerance & Exception Handling: Resilient error logging, network timeout handling, and automatic recovery.
4. Scalability & Performance: Ability to handle hundreds of concurrent hospital ward queries without latency degradation.
sub_questions.explanation: Throwaway prototypes model only the happy path of the user interface; non-functional architectural qualities require rigorous engineering.
